Find the Words

“How do I explain what I’m experiencing?”

Knowing how your body works is one thing. Explaining what’s happening in it, clearly enough that someone else understands, is another. This edition is about the words in between.

From the archive

This edition marks the first big shift in how Aletheia thought about health education. Young people told us they understood their bodies better after the first packs, but still froze in the GP’s office, or said “I just feel off” and watched the conversation move on. We realised knowledge needed language. This is where Voice Packs started becoming more than information sheets.

01

Before we begin

“I just feel off.”

You know something’s not right. But when someone asks what’s wrong, the words don’t come. You say “it hurts” or “I’m just tired”, and it sounds smaller than it feels.

That isn’t because your experience is small. It’s because nobody taught you the words for it. Doctors work with information: where, when, how bad, how often. The clearer the information, the easier it is for them, and for you, to work out what’s going on.

Your experience doesn’t need to be dramatic to be real. It needs to be described.

02

Learn

Health words, without the jargon

Some words come up in almost every appointment. Knowing them means you can follow what’s being said, and use them yourself.

Symptom

What it is
Something you notice that isn’t usual for you: pain, tiredness, a change in bleeding, a feeling that won’t shift.

Acute

What it is
Came on recently or suddenly. It doesn’t mean severe.

Chronic

What it is
Has lasted a long time, usually three months or more, or keeps coming back. It doesn’t mean it’s serious or can’t be helped.

Intermittent

What it is
Comes and goes, rather than being there all the time.

Referred pain

What it is
Pain you feel in one place that comes from somewhere else. Period pain often spreads to the lower back and thighs.

Fatigue

What it is
Exhaustion that doesn’t go away with rest. Different from being tired after a late night.

Dysmenorrhoea

dis-men-or-REE-a
What it is
The medical word for period pain. Primary means there’s no other condition causing it; secondary means there is.

Heavy menstrual bleeding

What it is
Bleeding that’s heavy enough to affect your day: changing a pad or tampon every one to two hours, flooding, or clots bigger than a 50-cent coin.

Irregular

What it is
Cycles that change a lot in length from one to the next, or are under 21 or over 45 days.

Words you might hear, and why it helps to know them

You don’t need to diagnose yourself. But knowing that some common conditions exist, and what they tend to look like, helps you recognise when something might be worth asking about.

Endometriosis

en-doh-mee-tree-OH-sis
What it is
Tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows outside it, causing inflammation and pain. About 1 in 7 people assigned female at birth in Australia are diagnosed by their late 40s.
What it can feel like
Period pain that stops you doing things, pain that gets worse over time, pain with bowel movements or weeing during your period, pain between periods.

You can say

  • My period pain stops me going to school.
  • It’s getting worse each year.

Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)

pol-ee-SIS-tik
What it is
A common hormonal condition, affecting about 8–13% of women of reproductive age. Despite the name, it isn’t about cysts.
What it can feel like
Irregular or missing periods, acne, extra hair on the face or body, or hair thinning on the head.
Updated
Archive note: in 2026 this condition was renamed polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). The current Voice Pack uses the new name.

You can say

  • My periods are often months apart.
  • I’ve had acne and irregular periods together for a while.

Iron deficiency

What it is
Not having enough iron, often because of heavy periods. It can lead to anaemia (low red blood cells).
What it can feel like
Tiredness that doesn’t lift, feeling breathless or dizzy, pale skin, finding it hard to concentrate.

You can say

  • I’ve been exhausted and my periods are heavy. Could we check my iron?

Premenstrual syndrome (PMS)

What it is
Physical and emotional changes in the days before a period: bloating, sore breasts, irritability, low mood. PMDD is a more severe form.
What it can feel like
A predictable dip in mood or energy that lifts once your period starts.

You can say

  • The week before my period, my mood drops a lot, every month.
03

Notice

Know your normal

Doctors often ask “Is this new?” or “Is this different for you?” To answer, you need a sense of your own baseline: what’s usual for your body.

Your baseline includes

  • How long your cycle usually is, and how many days you bleed
  • How heavy a normal day is for you
  • Your usual energy, sleep and appetite
  • How you usually feel emotionally across a month
  • Any pain you get regularly, and how bad it usually is

Signs of a change worth noticing

  • Something new that wasn’t there before
  • Something that’s getting worse over time
  • Something that’s stopping you doing things you normally do
  • Something that keeps coming back in a pattern
  • Something that other people have started noticing too

“Common” and “normal for you” aren’t the same thing. Lots of people get period pain. That doesn’t mean yours should stop you living your life.

Reflect

What’s your normal?

  1. How long is your cycle usually, roughly?
  2. On your heaviest day, how often do you change a pad, tampon or cup?
  3. What does a ‘normal’ energy day feel like for you?
  4. Is there anything that’s changed in the last few months?
04

Describe

Describe it: the five questions

Almost any symptom becomes clearer when you answer five questions. You don’t have to answer them perfectly. Even two or three makes a big difference.

The five questions for describing a symptom
Ask yourselfWhat it meansExample
1. What does it feel like?The type of feeling“A dull ache that turns sharp”
2. Where is it?The exact place, and whether it spreads“Low tummy, left side, spreads to my back”
3. When is it?When it started, when it happens, how long it lasts“Days 1–2 of my period, for about a year”
4. How much?How strong, and what it stops you doing“Usually a 6. I miss school on the first day”
5. What changes it?What makes it better or worse“Heat helps a bit. Moving makes it worse”

1 · What does it feel like? Words to try

Cramping

Squeezing or tightening, coming in waves.

Aching / dull

A heavy, constant, low-level pain.

Sharp / stabbing

Sudden, intense, in one spot.

Burning

Hot or stinging, like a burn.

Throbbing

Pulsing, like a heartbeat.

Pressure

Heavy, pushing or dragging down.

Shooting

Travels quickly down a leg or into your back.

Tender

Sore when touched or pressed.

2 · Where is it? Use the map

4 · How much? Rate what it stops you doing

Words for how you’re feeling inside

Mental and emotional symptoms need words too. “Stressed” and “sad” cover a lot. Try being more specific.

Instead of “stressed”

  • On edge, can’t switch off
  • Overwhelmed by small things
  • Heart racing, can’t catch my breath
  • Worrying most of the day

Instead of “sad”

  • Flat, like nothing matters
  • Numb, or disconnected
  • Crying more than usual
  • Not enjoying things I used to

Instead of “tired”

  • Exhausted even after sleeping
  • Brain fog, can’t concentrate
  • Everything takes more effort
  • Sleeping much more, or much less

And to say how long

  • Most days for the last two months.
  • Every month, in the week before my period.
  • It started after [something that happened] and hasn’t gone away.

Track it: patterns are information

05

Ask

Prepare, then ask

A GP appointment is often 10 to 15 minutes. Five minutes of preparing beforehand means you use that time well.

Before the appointment

  • Write your main concern in one sentence
  • Answer the five questions for it
  • Bring your tracker, or a few notes on your phone
  • List any medicines or supplements you take
  • Write down 2–3 questions
  • Ask for a longer appointment if you have more than one thing

Questions you’re allowed to ask

  • What could be causing this?
  • Is this something I should keep an eye on?
  • Are there tests that could help?
  • What can I do to feel better in the meantime?
  • What should make me come back sooner?
  • Can you write that down for me?
  • Could you explain that another way?

Booking the appointment

Receptionist
What’s the appointment for?
You
I’ve been having painful periods and I’d like to talk to a GP about it.
Receptionist
No problem. Do you need a standard or a long appointment?
You
Could I have a long one? I have a few things to go through.

You don’t have to give the receptionist details. “A private health concern” is enough.

Opening the appointment

Clinician
What brings you in today?
You
I’ve had period pain for about a year that’s getting worse. It’s sharp and cramping, low on my left side and into my back. It’s usually a 6, and on the first day it’s an 8, so I miss school.
You
Heat helps a bit, but not enough. I brought my tracker.

That’s thirty seconds, and it answers most of the questions the GP would otherwise need to ask.

Maya, one year later

From “it hurts” to a clear description

Maya’s cramps have got worse. Last time she told a school nurse “my stomach hurts on my period”, she was given a heat pack and sent back to class.

This time she tracks two cycles. She notes where the pain is (low, mostly left, into her back), how long it lasts (the first two days), how strong it is (usually a 6, an 8 on day one) and what it stops (she’s missed four school days this term).

At the GP she reads from her notes. The GP asks more questions, suggests a plan to try for three months, and asks her to come back with her tracker if it doesn’t help.

Maya is fictional. Her story continues in Edition 03.
06

Ask

Your words

The best words are the ones you’ll actually say. Use this space to find yours.

Reflect

Write it in your words

  1. Something I’ve been noticing is…
  2. It feels like…
  3. It’s been happening since…
  4. It stops me from…
  5. What I’d like to find out is…
✓

If the words still won’t come

It’s fine to hand your notes to the GP, or to say “I’ve written it down, can I read it to you?” Writing it first is not a weakness. It’s preparation.

Where this idea went next

From finding words to the tools we use now

Language became central to Aletheia. It shaped the Self-Advocacy Journal (with its symptom tracker) and our workshops, and it’s why we build resources in more than one language.
